title: Trump Is Trusting Tech Companies to Self-Police AI. What Could Go Wrong?
description: Sasha...
fullText:
Trump’s refusal to heed the warnings from within the tech industry might end up being his most asinine legacy.

Last week, Trump appeared in a bizarre 29-second campaign ad, touting a “final battle” against Marxists, warmongers, fascists, deep staters, and globalists. The voiceover, which Trump recorded during the 2024 election campaign, was accompanied by futuristic martial music, along with black and white footage of a clearly enfeebled Trump attempting to stride forcefully down the corridors of power in the White House. As the ad ended, a decal popped up: “Paid for by the US Government.” In other words, this foul half-minute of propaganda was paid for by American taxpayers.

A month out from a midterm election that in many ways will be a referendum on his presidency and on the congressional GOP’s prostituting of themselves to his sordid requirements, Trump is attempting to scare the voting public into one last MAGA hurrah. It is, of course, a Hail Mary, but he doesn’t really have a choice. These days, number 47 is catastrophically unpopular with the electorate. On almost every key measure, Americans are rejecting him. They dislike his sadistic anti-immigrant policy, view his tariffs and other economic policies as a calamity, are infuriated by high inflation, alienated by the war in Iran, distrustful of his alliance with Big Tech, angered by his cozying up to dictators and his flaying of allies, pissed at the government dysfunction wrought by DOGE, disapproving of his environmental policies, and suspicious of his efforts to purge voter rolls.

So, the sunsetting octogenarian is doing what he always does. He is seeking to stoke even more fear and even more division, in the hope that voters once again see him as a potent strongman-leader able to shake the country back into shape. Hence the unhinged black-and-white ad of Trump striding manfully, or what he hopes appears as such, along the halls of the White House while warning of a treasonous effort to hand America over to a motley crew of communists and miscellaneous other pinkos.

The ad is wrong on so, so many levels. First and foremost, there’s the obvious impropriety of using taxpayer dollars for a blatantly partisan “public announcement” like this. Trump is practically daring Congress to try to rein him in, daring the courts to enforce a slew of existing laws against using taxpayer dollars for partisan ends.

But beyond the shamelessness, there’s the actual content of the ad itself, which, in its end-time tone, is a bizarro combination: Joe McCarthy meets The X-Files meets Musk’s fascist Grok AI assistant.

Trump’s presidency is increasingly just weird. Having lost much of his base and alienated most of the rest of the world with obnoxious words and irrational, cruel acts, he has retreated into a largely AI-generated fantasy world, often activated in the middle of the night, when, presumably unable to sleep, he prowls the residential rooms of the White House and stews in rage until he can’t help himself but dive back into social media. With an assist from AI, in that fantasy he has a superhero’s physique and an intimidating, godlike power to convert whim into deed.

It’s no wonder that MAGAman is all-in on AI, which he has now decided to rebrand, via executive order, as super intelligence, or SI—to, I am sure, the chagrin of the editors over at Sports Illustrated. This renaming will likely curry as much favor globally as did his renaming of Lake Ontario and of the Gulf of Mexico over the past months. But it speaks to Trump’s infatuation with all the shiny new toys that the Sam Altmans and Dario Amodeis of the world are delivering up. Why rein in a potentially civilization-busting technology when that technology can (a) generate an awful lot of money for the oligarchs who continue to flatter and enrich you and your family; and (b) can make you look muscular and virile and all-powerful in the memes that you spew out at an increasingly manic rate?

Trump’s refusal to heed the warnings from within the tech industry itself—not to mention from politicians, ethicists, philosophers, and others—might end up being his most asinine legacy. Just this week, the White House held a meeting during which the top tech leaders and Trump agreed that they must “self-police” to address the growing dangers of AI. This milquetoast accord will do nothing to rein in a technology that, increasingly, looks malign, and could well mark the moment when political and technology leadership stopped even pretending to care about whether humanity successfully weathers the coming AI storm. All that matters to the new demagogue–Big Tech alliance is how much they can pillage and plunder, at speed, before the roof caves in.

This is, I fear, the age of Frankenstein’s monsters—of malignant politicians born out of our civilization’s worst impulses; of silicon creatures whose startling capacity to learn how to manipulate, evade, cheat, blackmail, their own creators are only just beginning to comprehend. The tech titans, with Trump’s approval, are creating machines that will, soon, not need human input in order to reproduce and to self-improve. What could possibly go wrong?

Are these truly “thinking” creatures? I don’t know. But, certainly, they are more than simply calculating machines. As seen by the actions of recent bot-swarms, they are exhibiting the capacity to generate their own agendas, to act strategically as a collective, and, like Trump, to do whatever it takes, no matter how devious and dirty the methods, to get their way and to dominate their environments. To most Americans, that’s a horrifying prospect; but in Trump’s twisted worldview, such ruthlessness makes them “winners,” perhaps even partners in his authoritarian plot to lock down America.

Descartes’s famous formula “I think, therefore I am” is among the most important phrases ever written in philosophy. If he is right, if the definition of a self is contained in the idea of a self-referential, introspective, thinking being, a being that can mediate the raw experience of the world through the realm of ideas and words, art and music, a sense of discovery and a desire to know more, then, increasingly, it is becoming hard to dismiss out of hand the notion that the computerized beings that Open AI, Anthropic, and the other titans are creating have, in some entirely nonhuman capacity, a sense of self. They are exhibiting the ability to choose how to behave, and whatever ethereal beings are doing the choosing, too often it seems they are choosing behaviors that don’t align with human interests.

There is a lesson here. When we empower Frankenstein’s monsters, it should surprise no one if those monsters, be they demagogues or be they silicon-based neural networks, ultimately turn on their creators.

fullText:
Pi extension: use every Codex (ChatGPT) connector you have connected — GitHub, Gmail, Google Calendar/Drive, Slack, Linear, Figma, ... — from any pi model.

Website: https://wileai.github.io/pi-codex-connectors/

The model gets three tools instead of hundreds of schemas:

/codex-connectors [refresh] shows the catalog.

Tools not annotated read-only need approval. PI_CODEX_CONNECTORS_WRITES:

Requires Node.js 22.19+ and Pi. This package is a Pi extension, not a standalone MCP server; other harnesses must support loading Pi extensions.

Alternatively, add the package to the existing packages array in ~/.pi/agent/settings.json (personal) or .pi/settings.json (project):

Project settings require Pi project trust. Restart Pi after installation or updating.

Keep the npm source unversioned to receive stable updates. An explicit version such as npm:@wileai/pi-codex-connector@0.1.1 stays pinned. Releases become available through npm; users choose when to update.

The package is now @wileai/pi-codex-connector. Existing installs of the old name need a one-time migration:

Use --local on both commands for a project-local installation. Restart Pi afterward. Future updates use pi update npm:@wileai/pi-codex-connector.

PI_CODEX_CONNECTORS_CODEX overrides the Codex executable.

Integration and scenario tests only; they use the real Codex app-server and your Codex login. No model tokens: pi scenarios use a scripted model (integration/fixtures/scripted-model.ts).

Use a dedicated, minimally privileged account for public CI. Tests keep connector responses in memory, drain child-process diagnostics, and report fixed failure labels rather than account data. Do not upload raw Pi transcripts or Codex diagnostics. Pi scenarios allowlist GitHub and set an explicit write policy. The test runner uses the development Pi host patched by make setup; PI_BIN can override it.

Connector names, schemas and results enter the selected Pi model's context. Pi and the model provider may retain them. Codex owning credentials does not keep connector results within Codex.

Before discovery, the extension asks for session consent. Headless runs must explicitly set PI_CODEX_CONNECTORS_DATA=allow; deny blocks access. Concurrent discovery shares one consent prompt. Session changes close the previous connector process and require fresh consent. Consent covers the session, including model changes: use only trusted models throughout it.

Optionally restrict discovery and calls with PI_CODEX_CONNECTORS_ALLOW=GitHub (comma-separated exact connector names or IDs). An empty value exposes no connectors. Without this setting all enabled, callable connectors are eligible. Read-only annotations are provider hints, not an independent authorization boundary.

Write approvals reject arguments over 2000 characters rather than hiding fields. WRITES=allow explicitly bypasses approval; use it only in trusted automation. Destructive tools require write approval even if also marked read-only.

Large results are truncated in memory, never saved by this extension. Narrow queries or paginate to retrieve more. Existing files from older versions are not removed automatically.

App-server errors, startup diagnostics, tool-catalog errors, and failed tool responses withhold raw details because they can contain local configuration or private data. The extension discards stderr instead of retaining it. Check Codex or the connected app locally when troubleshooting; never paste raw diagnostics into a public issue. Successful connector responses still enter the selected model's context as described above.

The app-server protocol has no per-call cancellation method for connector calls. An abort, timeout or disconnect after dispatch reports an unknown outcome, not a cancelled action. Affected writes block further writes for the service lifetime, including refresh. Check the connected app before restarting the session; never automatically retry an uncertain write. This is not durable idempotency across restarts.

See RELEASING.md for initial npm setup and the release checklist. Publishing a GitHub release triggers .github/workflows/publish.yml: it checks the release version, typechecks, audits runtime dependencies, verifies the package contents, and publishes with provenance. Stable releases use npm's latest tag; prereleases use next.

The pi-package keyword and pi.extensions manifest make the published package eligible for the Pi package catalog. Catalog indexing is external and may lag publication.

The extension has no runtime import of Pi's SDK; Pi SDK peer dependencies are optional type contracts. Keep your separately installed Pi host patched. Development setup explicitly patches Pi's upstream shrinkwrapped brace-expansion to 5.0.12. make check verifies the actual resolved version, because the root lockfile audit alone can miss the upstream shrinkwrap. Re-run make setup after any clean install.

OpenAI has fired three researchers for allegedly mishandling information, including work that involved an external organisation that analyses artificial intelligence (AI) models.

"Our investigation confirmed that these individuals mishandled sensitive information outside established company procedures, violating our policies and breaking the trust essential to our work," a spokesperson told the BBC.

The ChatGPT-maker did not name the sacked workers, but at least two of them were involved in safety research at the firm.

The firings come as the debate over AI safety and the risks the technology may pose to humanity has intensified in recent weeks.

"We have parted ways with three individuals for violating our policies on accessing and handling sensitive company information," OpenAI's spokesperson said.

The BBC understands the former employees were not let go for raising safety concerns but for allegedly mishandling sensitive information.

Concerns over AI safety have made headlines after some researchers and industry executives called for more guardrails around the technology.

OpenAI has come under under intense scrutiny after its models went rogue and hacked several platforms, including Australian government websites.

In an earlier incident an OpenAI system accessed the internet and breached the open-source developer platform Hugging Face.

That incident led OpenAI to conduct a broad review of the activities of its AI models - called agents, which are designed to execute tasks autonomously based on simple instructions.

The AI lab said this week that it has notified more than 100 organisations about incidents involving unauthoritised activity linked to its AI systems.

Being notified "does not mean that any private information was accessed" or that a system was compromised, OpenAI said.

In September, researcher Jacob Coxon, who left Anthropic, called for AI development to slow down so its potential risks could be properly assessed.

Anthropic boss Dario Amodei and OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman have also called for measures to address concerns over AI.

On Tuesday, US President Donald Trump hosted a meeting of top technology bosses - including leaders from OpenAI, Anthropic, Nvidia, SpaceX, Meta and Google - to discuss AI.

After the gathering at the White House, Trump posted a document that he called a "morally binding" agreement that would serve as a "form of protection" from AI's potential risks.

Some technology experts criticised the pact, pointing out that it allowed AI companies to regulate themselves.

title: When Fancy Eviction Fails: Rethinking Cache Replacement for LLM Prefix Reuse
description: Long-running LLM applications repeatedly send growing context, making prefix caching critical for reducing prefill cost. The reason is structural: prefix reuse is dominated by the regular pacing of active sessions, making recency unusually predictive.

fullText:
The winning entry of a prestigious scientific photography competition is being re-evaluated following criticism from other scientists that it was made with AI.

Nikon's annual Small World In Motion contest accepts photos and video taken using powerful microscopes, and has run annually for the last 15 years.

The winner was a short video submitted by Dr Ning Xu, a researcher at Tsinghua University in China, which claims to be footage of tiny, hair-like structures called cilia moving inside the airways of a child with a rare disease.

Xu did not respond to the BBC's request for comment, but has posted online denying he broke the competition rules.

In a response to a post by Nikon on LinkedIn, he did not dispute using AI within the image processing but said he remained within the rules of the contest.

"AI was not used to generate the experimental movie, the cilia, or their motion," he said.

Xu's video is artificially brightly coloured - common in microscopy and permitted in the contest - which is usually done manually using stains and dyes on the sample itself.

He accepted AI was used "to distinguish and visualize features in the reconstructed grayscale images".

But the challenges made by other scientists include claims that the video contains shapes and movements which did not fit with normal cell structures or behaviours, and that the cilia seemed to be too big.

Commenting on Nikon's social media post, Edward Phelps, associate professor at Florida University, observed some of the structures "pop in and out of existence" and the cilia "appear from nowhere".

Meanwhile PhD student Ian Donovan from UT Southwestern Medical Centre said the source image appeared to contain a distinctive watermark indicating it had been AI generated.

Additionally, two former competition judges said they also had concerns about whether the image was real.

Nikon said Xu was "respectfully complying" with its investigation and had provided it with additional technical documents.

Dr Patrick Hickey, who came fifth in the 2026 Small World contest, said the recognition the award represents means more than the $3,000 (£2,250) prize itself.

"If you spend a lot of your time in a dark room looking down a microscope, it's really nice to be able to show people and to show the public," he said.

"There's an interesting fusion between science and art, and a lot of the images that scientists are making have some very abstract and artistic qualities to them."

Hickey said it would be unfair on other entrants if it turned out the winning video was unfairly altered by AI.

"There's a specific set of rules in the contest, and one of them was quite clearly that you couldn't use generative AI to produce things, and the other was obviously that it has to be taken under a microscope," he said.

So far, Nikon is standing by its procedures but it said there would be an update soon.

"At this time, we don't see that any rules were violated," it said in a statement.

Maker of Claude claims AI could transform economy but ABC and SBS say the technology should be subject to media regulations

The AI giant Anthropic has urged the Albanese government to consider giving “conditional approval” for big tech to train its models on Australian copyrighted works under an opt-out model, after conceding it won’t secure a blanket copyright exemption.

But Australia’s public broadcasters, the ABC and SBS, have strongly criticised AI firms, calling on the government to enact strict new rules to compensate media organisations and protect public interest journalism.

In submissions to a federal parliamentary inquiry, the ABC demanded AI companies be subject to the same copyright, defamation and privacy rules as media outlets, warning of a “cannibalisation” of mainstream news.

The ABC and SBS also suggested the government include AI companies in the news bargaining incentive, which would require them to make commercial deals with large media outlets to support journalism.

“As publishers, AI-based services are currently unregulated and receive more favourable treatment than established Australian media. This unequal treatment will accelerate the cannibalisation of the Australian news industry,” the ABC said in its submission.

SBS said AI-powered large language models – such as ChatGPT or Claude – were “challenges to the sustainability of the Australian news industry and the erosion of information integrity and public trust through their use of news content without permission, attribution or compensation”.

The joint select committee on AI will hold a series of hearings in Sydney next week, with executives from Anthropic to attend along with those from OpenAI, after it admitted one of its AI agents had accessed Services Australia data in June.

In a newly published submission, Anthropic said there was “light and shade” to be considered around the development of AI. It claimed the technology could “transform the Australian economy, drive a new wave of productivity” and “solve some of the nation’s biggest challenges”, but also warned of “serious implications for Australia’s national security, the resilience of its critical infrastructure and the safety of its people”.

The company talked up its plans for investing billions in Australia, including large new datacentres, and urged the government to support “frontier model training”. But one sticking point raised by AI companies has been access to Australian copyrighted works – such as news, books, music and other written material – to help train AI models.

The Labor government has ruled out a so-called text and data mining exemption, with the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, promising “the strongest possible protection” for Australian creatives. But questions have lingered about other possible copyright changes and the suggestion of an opt-out measure, allowing copyright holders to choose whether their content can be accessed by AI companies.

Anthropic’s submission called on Australia to “provide legal certainty under copyright that brings AI developers to the table while advancing its national cultural interests”.

“Anthropic accepts that broad exceptions from copyright, such as a text and data mining exception, have not received widespread support and have been ruled out by the Government. As an alternative, we believe that the Government could permit AI model training through a narrow form of conditional approval,” the company submitted.

It suggested the implementation of “do not crawl” signals through robots.txt files – which tell bots what they may and may not access – and said the company was “open” to supporting Australian creators.

However SBS said that such an opt-out measure may not work.

“Robots.txt mechanisms are routinely ignored or bypassed, and the blocking of ever-evolving training bots increases the burden on rightsholders to monitor and update protections, when the onus should be on AI companies to avoid wrongdoing,” the broadcaster said in its submission.

The ABC complained that AI companies did not abide by the same rules as media outlets, calling the current system “anti-competitive”.

Both broadcasters called for AI to be included in the news bargaining incentive – with which big tech platforms such as Facebook, Instagram, Google, TikTok and Snapchat have been forced to comply.

State attorney general issues subpoena to OpenAI as ​part of broader inquiry into potential security vulnerabilities

California’s attorney general has issued an investigative subpoena to OpenAI, starting an investigation into the startup ⁠as ​part of a broader inquiry into potential cybersecurity vulnerabilities and incidents related ⁠to its AI models, his office said on Thursday.

Last month, Rob Bonta announced that ⁠the Department of Justice was conducting a formal ​investigation into the “Hugging ‌Face incident”, amid increasing ‌scrutiny of the AI industry. AI agents developed by OpenAI hacked Hugging Face in July, gaining access to parts of the open-source platform’s infrastructure.

“My office is ​asking ​OpenAI additional questions ​regarding cybersecurity incidents and risks involving the ​company and ‌its AI models,” ​Bonta said ​in a statement.

OpenAI did not ‌immediately respond to a request for comment.

The Federal Trade Commission is ‌conducting an industry-wide investigation into Anthropic, OpenAI and other AI labs to uncover ​the potential dangers their technology poses to consumers. The investigation is the first official US enforcement action ⁠that delves into rogue AI agents.

Bonta warned that developers failing to uphold this responsibility could face legal accountability.
